newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARIAN INDUSTRIALISTS PESSIMISTIC IN 1997 - SURVEY.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARIAN INDUSTRIALISTS PESSIMISTIC IN 1997 - SURVEY.

text.p: The bulk of Hungary's top industrialists do not expect an improvement in their results in 1997, a recent survey showed.

The research, carried out last November for Austrian advisor company Czipin & Partner by Marketing Centrum National Market Research Institute, surveyed the managers of 200 industrial companies with a workforce of at least 300.
"Eighty percent of companies do not expect any changes either positively or negatively," Klaus Harrer, Czipin & Partner's managing director told a news conference on Thursday.
"Only eleven percent expect their results to improve and nine percent expect a deterioration," a written summary of the survey said.
Development is hampered mainly by state burdens and continuously rising energy and raw material costs, while wage rises and financial factors have less impact, the survey showed.
Those managers looking forward to a better performance in 1997, believe that streamlining was the key to improvement.

"Managers feel the profitability of their companies could improve mainly as a result of rationalisation, while they expect little from the launch of new products or from search for new clients and markets," it said.
Twenty-five percent of companies surveyed planned to improve their performance by streamlining their activities in 1997, the survey said.
It added that 31 percent of companies hade reported substantial records on this area while 64 percent had seen only minor improvements by streamlining.
Only 15 percent of companies look forward to increased sales on the back of new clients or new products, it said.
One in four companies plans to spend fresh money on machinery while 63 percent have benefited little from new investments so far.
"Overall we can say Hungarian industrial companies' managers substantially underestimate reserves within their companies to boost results," Harrer said in the statement.
